writing.explanation:
At time 0 only job 0 with duration 3 is available, so it finishes first. At time 3 jobs 1 and 2 are ready; duration 1 beats duration 2. The completion order is 0,1,2; jobs are never interrupted mid-run.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse unique job IDs with arrival t and positive duration d. Run the shortest available job nonpreemptively, breaking equal durations by smaller ID. Return completion order. The visible fixture is `(id0,t0,d3),(id1,t1,d1),(id2,t1,d2)` and its example result is `0,1,2`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Priority Scheduling when it asks for task scheduling, CPU queues, simulation. Here the concrete task is: Parse unique job IDs with arrival t and positive duration d. Run the shortest available job nonpreemptively, breaking equal durations by smaller ID. Return completion order. The visible input `(id0,t0,d3),(id1,t1,d1),(id2,t1,d2)` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Use it when only top-ranked candidates or repeated next-best extraction matters; sorting the entire stream may waste work. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Order available work by the decision criterion while time controls when work becomes eligible. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A heap keeps the current extremum accessible while new items arrive. Explain what belongs in the heap and what may be discarded. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n log n) time · O(n) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `0,1,2` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check an empty stream, k equal to zero or to the input length, duplicate priorities, and stale entries if deletion is lazy. Rust `BinaryHeap` is a max-heap; Reverse can express a min-heap. Keep the heap's ordering key separate from unrelated payload data. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
